source.title: Empowering Large Language Models in Wireless Communication: A Novel Dataset and Fine-Tuning Framework
source.authors: Yushen Lin; Ruichen Zhang; Wenqi Huang; Kaidi Wang; Zhiguo Ding; Daniel K. C. So; Dusit Niyato

record.file_problem: Not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends scaling investigations to wireless-domain fine-tuning and reports performance changes with data-subset size and LoRA rank, but does not measure the pretraining-loss power laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task-performance gains from fine-tuning, not held-out cross-entropy loss. It does not fit or test a power law in parameter count, tokens, or compute, extrapolate loss, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its data-size and rank results are recorded as related findings, not as measurements of the claim versions. It also reports fine-tuning comparisons in Figs. 3–4 and downstream-task results, but those do not test the loss-scaling claims.
record.test_reason: Section VI-A, 'Scaling Laws', only plots LoRA fine-tuning task performance gain against training-subset size (1–20%) and LoRA rank (8/16/32) for three models. No loss is measured, no power law is fitted, and nothing is extrapolated or allocated by compute. The authors describe diminishing returns and a ceiling only in words. This is a related construct (fine-tuning accuracy gain against data fraction), not a test of any version, including V5's power-law form for fine-tuning. The record's T3/'tests' is not supported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say more fine-tuning data helps, but returns diminish after about 10–15% and approach a ceiling, so data quality matters. They say larger LoRA rank gives limited gains, so small r suits constrained devices. Their 'scaling laws' claim rests on these curves, not on any fitted law. Their main conclusions concern the dataset and PVI-based fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies LoRA fine-tuning on a wireless-communication dataset using task-performance gains; it does not use the original studies’ held-out pretraining-loss scaling and compute-allocation measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance is examined across training-data subset size and LoRA rank. The paper reports diminishing returns after about 10-15% of the data and limited gain from increasing rank.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA fine-tuning performance gain on a wireless Q&A dataset rises with training-subset size, with diminishing returns after about 10–15% of the data. Increasing LoRA rank gives limited benefit. Larger models show larger gains (LLaMA-2 7B > GPT-2 XL > GPT-2 Large).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain fine-tuning task gains increase with fine-tuning data fraction with diminishing returns, and depend little on LoRA rank.

fits_no_version.finding: Table II: zero-shot accuracy on the wireless dataset broadly rises with model size across GPT/LLaMA/OPT families, with exceptions (TinyLLaMA 1.1B 0.378 vs LLaMA-2 7B 0.124). The authors attribute the exceptions to LLaMA-2's poor instruction-following.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-family downstream accuracy is not monotone in parameter count on specialised domain QA.

record.code_released: https://github.com/GTMANChopin/Study-in-Wireless-LLM (the paper says the dataset and code will be released there)
record.problems: No loss metric or scaling-law fit is reported for the claim; plotted Fig. 8 values are not tabulated, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The reported data-subset performance gains are task-specific fine-tuning outcomes, not held-out pretraining losses.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported subset-size values in Fig. 3 or the rank/model curves in Fig. 8 were omitted. Other fine-tuning comparison and downstream-task results were not included because they do not measure a claim version or the scaling behavior recorded under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured and no power law in parameters, tokens or compute is fitted.
No comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count.
Fine-tuning data scaling is plotted only as accuracy-type gain; no loss is measured and no power-law form is fitted or tested.
Table II compares accuracy across mixed model families without a scaling fit and without pretraining loss; downstream predictability is not tested.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'scaling laws' loosely. Table II has inconsistencies: GPT-2 XL is listed twice (774M and 1.5B), and OPT-350M is mentioned in the text but absent from the table. Fig. 3 values are not strictly monotone (e.g. GPT-2 XL at 3% is 8.639, at 4% is 8.591). There are no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run loss fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is measured.
No controlled architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.

The paper examines fine-tuning performance versus data-subset size and LoRA rank, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit/test whether the same power-law form holds. It does not examine other modalities, repeated-data training, or transfer.
No relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance, or downstream predictability from scale, is tested.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or dependence of either on parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting method is evaluated.
